content: 1. Health-based targets should be established to manage health risks effectively. 2. Health protection measures must be implemented to achieve these health-based targets. 3. Systematic assessment and monitoring are essential to ensure the effectiveness of these measures. 4. The primary health hazards associated with the use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater in agriculture and aquaculture include excreta-related pathogens, certain vector-borne diseases, and specific chemicals. 5. Health risks are defined as the probability that these hazards will adversely affect human health under specific circumstances. 6. Pathogens can survive in the environment (e.g., wastewater, water, soil, crops) long enough to remain viable and transmissible to humans. 7. Some pathogens are capable of multiplying in the environment. 8. Environmental factors such as time, temperature, moisture, light exposure, ultraviolet (UV) radiation, the presence of intermediate hosts, and plant type influence the survival and die-off of pathogens. 9. In many developing countries, wastewater treatment is not a feasible option, necessitating non-treatment approaches to prevent pathogen transmission or exposure to hazardous chemicals. 10. These non-treatment measures require regulators to adapt strategies based on time and location-specific conditions. 11. Regulatory frameworks must translate broad policy guidance on hazard identification into system-specific actions. These actions should focus on concrete hazards and deploy effective health protection measures to eliminate or reduce their negative effects. 12. Depending on local circumstances, health hazards associated with wastewater, excreta, and greywater use may evolve into health risks. 13. The level of risk is influenced by environmental and social determinants and is based on available evidence. 14. Outbreaks of diseases such as cholera, typhoid, and dysentery have been linked to the use of wastewater, excreta, or greywater for vegetable irrigation. 15. Pathogens that survive long enough in the environment to pose health risks necessitate health protection measures such as disinfection, washing, and cooking of produce. 16. Soil-transmitted helminths (e.g., Ascaris, Ancylostoma, Necator, Trichuris, Taenia spp.) pose significant risks in agriculture, especially where untreated wastewater and excreta are used, and sanitation standards are low. 17. Helminth eggs can survive in the environment for extended periods. 18. Hookworm infections (e.g., Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus) are common in areas where farmers do not wear adequate footwear. 19. Trematode parasites (e.g., Clonorchis, Opisthorchis, Fasciola, Schistosoma spp.) are a major risk in aquaculture, particularly in regions where these parasites are endemic. 20. Foodborne trematodes are transmitted through the consumption of raw or undercooked fish, while schistosomiasis is spread through skin contact with contaminated freshwater. 21. Protozoa (e.g., Giardia, Cyclospora, Cryptosporidium, Entamoeba spp.) have been found on wastewater-irrigated vegetables at harvest and in markets. 22. Protozoa can survive in the environment long enough to pose health risks. 23. Viruses (e.g., hepatitis A and E, adenovirus, rotavirus, norovirus) are present in high numbers in wastewater and excreta. Some can survive in the environment long enough to pose health risks. 24. Crop contamination with viruses has been linked to disease outbreaks. 25. Vector-borne diseases (e.g., dengue virus, Japanese encephalitis virus) are a risk in areas where water resource development activities occur. Most insect vectors breed in clean water, except for those transmitting lymphatic filariasis, which breed in organically polluted water. 26. Skin irritants, such as those causing contact dermatitis (eczema), are likely due to a combination of microbial and chemical hazards. 27. Chemicals such as antibiotics (e.g., chloramphenicol) and cyanobacterial toxins (e.g., microcystin-LR) pose potential risks to consumers of aquacultural products. 28. Heavy metals (e.g., arsenic, cadmium, lead, mercury) may accumulate in plants, both aquatic and terrestrial. 29. Phthalates and phenols have been found in aquifers recharged through wastewater irrigation and may have endocrine-disrupting properties. 30. Halogenated hydrocarbons (e.g., dioxins, furans, PCBs) are not absorbed by plants but may contaminate surfaces if plants are not peeled or washed before consumption. 31. Waste-fed aquaculture can lead to contamination of fish and plants with human excreta-related pathogens on their surfaces and, in the case of fish, in their intestines. 32. Microbial penetration of edible fish tissues may occur under stressful conditions (e.g., low dissolved oxygen, high ammonia concentrations, overcrowding). However, contamination levels are generally insignificant compared to contamination during unhygienic fish cleaning or processing. 33. Trematode transmission to humans can occur if infected feces, suitable intermediate hosts (e.g., aquatic snails), and raw or inadequately cooked fish or plants are present. 34. In areas where these conditions exist, the presence or absence of viable trematode eggs in fish ponds serves as a suitable microbial water quality indicator. 35. Communities practicing waste-fed aquaculture may experience measurable health impacts due to heavy contact with waste-fed ponds and consumption of fish raised in these ponds. 36. Farmers of aquatic plants in wastewater-contaminated ponds often develop skin diseases such as contact dermatitis. 37. Exposure to untreated feces is always unsafe due to the potential presence of high levels of disease-causing organisms, including bacteria, viruses, parasitic protozoa, and helminths. 38. These organisms primarily cause infectious diseases affecting the gastrointestinal system. 39. Enteric viruses are now considered the leading cause of gastrointestinal infections in industrialized countries. 40. In rural areas of many developing countries, open defecation and the use of untreated feces are often associated with the transmission of intestinal worms, particularly among children under 15 years of age engaged in agricultural activities. 41. The use of source-separated urine in agriculture generally entails low health risks, as pathogens in urine die off quickly under recommended storage conditions. 42. Most health risks associated with urine use stem from cross-contamination with fecal material. 43. Risks can be minimized by storing urine in a sealed tank or container for one to six months, depending on the crops to be fertilized and the ambient temperature. 44. The use of greywater in agriculture and aquaculture poses lower health risks than wastewater and fecal material. However, risks related to fecal cross-contamination may still exist and can be mitigated through health protection measures or adequate treatment. 45. Estimating the level of disease associated with the use of wastewater, excreta, and greywater can be challenging due to the multifactorial nature of outcomes, which result from multiple transmission pathways or exposures. 46. Diarrhea and intestinal helminth infections are often measured as general indicators of excreta-related diseases. 47. Diseases related to chemical exposures are harder to detect due to their complex and multifactorial nature.
